title: Google’s finally bringing this desktop Meet accessibility tool to mobile
summary: Tile pairing lets you keep meeting participants locked together on your screen.
body: TL;DR Google Meet introduced tile pairing for desktop in 2023, letting you lock two participant windows together. Paired tiles are ideal for working with an interpreter, especially for sign language. Support has now started rolling out to Android, with iOS joining in early November. Whether you got into them keeping up with your work team over pandemic, or just like to check in face-to-face with extended family, most of us have had plenty of chances to participate in video conferences by now. As such, you probably know just how dynamic the bigger ones can be, with participants sliding around and grabbing focus when they turn on their cameras, lead the chat, or share their screens. But sometimes it makes sense to put some limits on some of those changes, and today Google’s sharing an important Meet upgrade along those lines when it comes to accessibility. Three years ago, Google introduced a new Meet feature for desktops: tile pairing. The idea is that if one participant needs another’s help, like if they’re acting as an interpreter — and sign language is probably the obvious use-case here — Meet can lock their tiles together to act as a set. title: Your car may no longer need your phone to get the full Spotify experience
summary: The new Spotify native in-car app brings videos, lyrics, and smarter playback straight to your dashboard.
body: TL;DR Spotify has launched its first fully native in-car app built on Android Automotive OS, debuting in select Audi vehicles. Unlike Android Auto, the new app works without a connected phone and supports Spotify Jam, DJ, music videos, real-time lyrics, and hands-free voice controls. The app is rolling out to supported Audi models across 47 markets, with more automakers expected to join over the coming year. Google has been giving in-car entertainment a major push this year, from redesigning Android Auto’s music player to expanding the selection of apps available in vehicles with Google built-in. Now, Spotify is taking things further by giving drivers an entirely new way to enjoy their music without relying on their phones. Spotify announced today that its first fully native in-car app, built on Android Automotive OS , is rolling out to select Audi vehicles. Unlike Android Auto, which projects apps from your smartphone onto the dashboard, Android Automotive runs directly on the vehicle’s infotainment system. This means Spotify can launch and play music without connecting your phone through Bluetooth or a cable.
